html:
The Old Babylonian kingdom was the first state ruled from Babylon, from about 1894 to 1595 BCE, and the kingdom of Hammurabi. Its kings were Amorites, whose people had moved into Mesopotamia after the fall of Ur III. The dates follow the Middle Chronology and are still debated.

For its first century Babylon was one small city among many. That changed under Hammurabi, who reigned from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. Through alliances and war he defeated his rivals, among them Larsa in the south and Mari on the Euphrates, and ruled almost all of Mesopotamia.

  • He issued the Code of Hammurabi, carved on a stone stele.
  • Babylon's god Marduk rose to be the chief god of the land.
  • Scribal schools copied Sumerian classics and wrote new ones; the Akkadian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh dates from this time.
  • Babylonian mathematics, using numbers in base sixty, reached a high level, with tables of squares and work on right-angled triangles.

After Hammurabi the kingdom shrank. The far south broke away, and the state lived on in northern Babylonia. In about 1595 BCE the Hittite king Mursili I made a long-distance raid and sacked Babylon, ending the dynasty. The Kassites, a people from the Zagros mountains, took over and ruled for more than four centuries. Babylon itself kept its prestige as the holy and learned city of Mesopotamia.
